newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia and Gulf increasing ties because of crude oil.
newsitem.headline: Asia and Gulf increasing ties because of crude oil.

text.p: The booming energy market of Asia and the Gulf's large crude reserves are increasing the two region's dependence on one another, Saudi Oil Minister Ali al-Naimi said on Tuesday.

"East Asia needs oil for economic growth, the Gulf needs this market for sales and the geographic proximity makes the two ideally connected," he told delegates at the 12th Asia-Pacific Petroleum Conference.
But Naimi said Saudi Arabia was pressing to move beyond interdependence to closer economic ties, through joint ventures.
The Middle East, which sits on more than 65 percent of the world's crude oil reserves, provides almost 10 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude to Asia.
Saudi Arabia alone sold four million bpd of crude to Asia, Naimi said.
"However, we expect that this volume and percentage will grow in the next few years. Asia's location makes it the best market for Saudi oil and Saudi Arabia the best source of oil for Asia," he said.
Saudi Arabia is the world's biggest crude oil exporter and dominant member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
Asia's demand for oil is expected to balloon as the economies and populations in the region grow. Most of that demand is expected to be met from the Middle East.
Subroto, Indonesia's former OPEC Secretary General, told the conference the world population was expected to grow to 7.8 billion by 2020 from 5.7 billion in 1995.
Half the world's population would be in Asia, where 1.1 billion people would be added between 1995 and 2020, he said.
In 1990, Asia's share of world output was 25 percent, Subroto said. By 2000 it was expected to be 35 percent and by 2020 it was expected to surpass the United States and Europe.
That would result in Asian oil consumption of 25.3 million barrels per day (bpd) by 2000 compared with 17.9 million bpd in 1995.
Naimi said Saudi Arabia could meet Asia's growing demands but it wanted to move to closer economic ties with consumers.
"Integration means stability and rising living standards. It bears even more fruit with the right partners," he said.

In 1994, Saudi Aramco, the kingdom's state-owned oil group, acquired a 40 percent stake for $502 million in Petron Corp, the biggest Philippines oil refiner and distributor. In 1991 it took a stake in Ssangyong Oil of South Korea.
Naimi said Saudi Arabia was exploring investments in India and China, but he declined to talk about how the negotiations were progressing.

Saudi Arabia is negotiating with China's state oil group SINOCHEM on setting up a 200,000 bpd refinery in the eastern province of Shandong. Chinese oil officials say the talks centre on the degree of Aramco's access to the giant China market and on financing the project.
Aramco is also in talks over the expansion of an existing plant in Guangdong.
The Indian government has approved plans for Aramco to link up with state-owned Hindustan Petroleum Corp for a 120,000 bpd refinery project in the northern state of Punjab.
Saudi Aramco's current ventures, which include refineries in the United States and Greece, absorb 1.5 million bpd of its crude oil.
The ventures with China and India would tie up more of Saudi Arabia's crude exports of almost seven million bpd.
